newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian Parliament approves gold coin sale plan.
newsitem.headline: Belgian Parliament approves gold coin sale plan.

text.p: Belgium's parliament approved on Thursday a government plan to raise the amount of central bank gold that can be sold in the form of commemorative coins.

The government proposal, made in a draft law bringing the statutes of the National Bank of Belgium (NBB) into line with requirements for European economic and monetary union (EMU), raises by approximately 133 tonnes the amount of central bank gold that can be sold in this way.
Coin sales would be limited to a maximum 26 tonnes a year and have to be approved first by the planned European Central Bank, the law says.
The proceeds, less a share belonging to Luxembourg, could only be used to repay Belgium's foreign currency debt, it adds.

The new law replaces a previous statute permitting the Belgian central bank to sell up to 36 tonnes of gold in the form of coins. So far the bank has used approximately 29 tonnes of that facility, although is in the process at the moment of selling a new series of commemorative gold "euro" coins.
Here follows a Reuter translation of the text of the gold coin part of the statutes:

"The Bank is authorised, on condition of clearance by the ECB, to issue gold coins, having legal tender, for numismatic or commemorative use, to the equivalent of 10 percent of the weight of gold in the Bank's assets at January 1, 1987; it can only use however a maximum of two percent of this weight of gold per year.

"The net product of the issue of these coins, less the recognised amount due to the Luxembourg State by the protocol relative to the monetary association between the two states of March 9, 1981, is to be transferred to the State. The share which is due to (the State) must have the effect of reducing its debt in currencies."
Central bank officials have previously said the bank held 1,329 tonnes of gold at the beginning of 1987. It has since sold around 733 tonnes.
